precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: A new Precision Nutrition Level 1 client wants a complete diet by Friday. What is your first coaching move?

options.a: Help them notice current eating and pick one small next action
options.b: Hand over a 12-week contest menu with macros for every meal
options.c: Start a 30-day elimination diet to find hidden food triggers
options.d: Set a weekly pound-loss quota so they feel urgency from day one

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: PN Level 1 is client-centered: first build awareness of what they already do, then one small, owned action. Dumping a contest meal plan, an elimination protocol, or an imposed scale quota is expert-centered prescription, closer to meal-plan sales or medical nutrition therapy than coaching.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coaching with a day-one meal-plan dump; a full contest menu overloads a new client and skips awareness.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a clinical elimination protocol with a first coaching step; that work belongs with an RDN, not week-one habits.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an imposed outcome target with a first action; PN starts with behaviors the client can control.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: A client texts after a wedding weekend: “I blew it. I’m a failure.” What should you do first?

options.a: Restart the whole program from week one as a clean reset
options.b: Get curious about what happened and what still went well
options.c: Add extra cardio this week to offset the weekend calories
options.d: Tighten their weekend calorie cap so it cannot happen again

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Treat the weekend as data, not drama. Curiosity shows what got in the way, what they still did, and what to adjust. Shame, program restarts, compensatory training, or tighter restriction after a lapse all feed all-or-nothing thinking instead of outcome-based coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses one hard weekend with total program failure; restarting from scratch discards useful data and progress.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses nutrition coaching with CPT ‘earn it back’ programming; extra cardio frames food as a debt to punish.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a lapse with a reason to restrict harder; tighter caps after a blowout often drive the next one.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: You have a week of check-in data: walks were skipped, sleep was poor, and the scale is noisy. Outcome-based decision making says you:

options.a: Keep the original plan frozen until the 12-week reassessment
options.b: Choose the next step only from their original intake goals
options.c: Adjust the next action from what they did and how they feel
options.d: Change the plan after two down days on the bathroom scale

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Outcome-based decisions use recent behaviors, recovery, and how the client feels—not the plan on paper. You change the next small action from that evidence. Waiting 12 weeks, clinging to intake wishes, or reacting to two noisy scale days all ignore the data you already have.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a long program calendar with outcome-based coaching; freezing the plan for 12 weeks ignores live data.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses intake wishes with current evidence; starting goals set direction, not the next weekly action.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses two-day scale noise with a meaningful outcome; PN weighs habits, sleep, and performance over time.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: Which first habit best fits a Precision Nutrition Level 1 start?

options.a: A full meal plan they must follow at breakfast, lunch, and dinner
options.b: Three new habits at once so they feel early momentum this week
options.c: Daily calorie tracking in an app before any other coaching work
options.d: One clear, small, repeatable behavior they can do on a weekday

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Simple and sequential: one clear behavior they can repeat on an ordinary day (protein at breakfast, a 10-minute walk). A full meal plan, a three-habit stack, or mandatory calorie logging are multi-skill loads that crush early adherence.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a first habit with a whole-diet prescription; a meal plan is many behaviors at once, not one practice.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses momentum with stacking; several new habits at once lowers follow-through under 5S sequential coaching.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a high-effort tracking skill with a first habit; logging every calorie is rarely week-one work.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: Two useful habits compete and the client is already overloaded. You:

options.a: Pick the one they can still do on a genuinely bad day
options.b: Pick the one with the biggest predicted fat-loss impact
options.c: Pick the one you personally think matters most as coach
options.d: Run both habits this week and see which one sticks first

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Early 5S coaching prefers simple and supported: the habit that survives a bad day beats the theoretically ‘best’ habit. Coach preference and dual-habit experiments add friction. Adherence on a hard day is the filter.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses theoretical fat-loss impact with doability; the highest-yield habit fails if it dies under stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses expert-centered ranking with client-centered sizing; your priority is not their confidence.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a test with focus; running competing habits dilutes effort instead of choosing the sustainable one.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: A client will not log food in an app. How can you still coach nutrition behaviors?

options.a: Give a rigid meal plan so they never have to choose foods
options.b: Use plate photos, hand portions, or a one-item checklist
options.c: Rely on weekly weigh-ins as the only progress measure you review
options.d: Wait to start coaching until they agree to daily logging

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Meet them where they are. Plate methods, photos, hand portions, and single-item checklists still create awareness without requiring a food log. A rigid menu, scale-only reviews, or refusing to coach until they log all raise the barrier instead of lowering it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses refusal to log with a reason for a stricter menu; a full plan is usually a bigger demand than tracking.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses body weight with behavior data; the scale misses the habits photos or checklists can still capture.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one tracking method with readiness to be coached; logging is optional, not an entry ticket.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: Every new habit meets pushback in session. In PN coaching that resistance usually means:

options.a: Motivation is low, so raise the stakes with public deadlines
options.b: The plan is too easy, so you should add more challenge right away
options.c: Ambivalence is present; explore it with questions, not a lecture
options.d: They are noncompliant, so restate the program rules more clearly

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Resistance is usually mixed feelings, not laziness. Better questions surface change talk; lectures, public pressure, extra challenge, and rule recitals all escalate pushback. Client-centered coaching treats ambivalence as information.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses ambivalence with a motivation deficit you can scare away; deadlines often raise resistance.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses pushback with boredom; resistance more often means the ask is too big or not wanted.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses coaching with compliance policing; restating rules is a lecture, not motivational interviewing.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: How should a PN coach handle a request for body progress photos?

options.a: Make photos mandatory at intake before coaching can begin at all
options.b: Treat signup as consent to share before-and-after shots
options.c: Take the photos yourself in the gym after each session
options.d: Keep them optional, private, and used only with consent

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Body photos are optional, stored privately, and used only with specific consent. Payment, intake, or a coach-held camera does not authorize capture or posting. Client-centered coaching protects body autonomy and never makes photos a condition of help.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a useful metric with a coaching condition; mandatory photos ignore consent and body-image risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses paying for coaching with permission to publish images; sharing needs separate, explicit consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coach control with client control; gym-hallway photos after every session remove their choice.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: A client has missed three weekly check-ins in a row. Your best next step is to:

options.a: Reach out with a short, kind note that makes rejoining easy
options.b: Pause their account until they email an apology for missing
options.c: Send a reminder of the commitment they signed at onboarding
options.d: Assign extra habits so they catch up on all missed weeks

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Re-engagement is the skill: a short, kind, low-friction invite back. Ghosting, guilt about the contract, or extra homework after a lapse all raise the cost of returning. Shrink the next ask so they can re-enter this week.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a pause with coaching; freezing the account without a warm reach-out is effectively ghosting.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a signed form with re-engagement; pointing to the contract adds guilt instead of a path back.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses missed weeks with a reason to add load; extra habits punish the client who is already struggling.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: Weight is unchanged, but the client slept better and cooked three dinners. Why mention those wins?

options.a: The scale remains the only outcome that truly counts here
options.b: Behaviors and energy often shift before the scale moves
options.c: Non-scale wins distract from fat loss and should be ignored
options.d: Wins should stay hidden until the fat-loss goal is fully met

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Non-scale victories keep the feedback loop alive. Sleep, cooking, energy, and skill often move before weight. Celebrating those behaviors is outcome-based, not a distraction. Scale-only coaching trains clients to quit when the number is noisy.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses one biomarker with the whole outcome set; PN tracks behaviors, energy, and skills, not only weight.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses process wins with a side show; ignoring them removes the data that usually precedes fat loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses delayed praise with discipline; hiding wins until a goal weight kills the reinforcement loop.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: After a ‘perfect’ eating week the client rebounds. What is more useful than chasing perfect weeks?

options.a: Strict weekdays followed by an unrestricted weekend reward
options.b: Two perfect days each week with no plan for the other five
options.c: An 80–90 percent week they can repeat without a rebound
options.d: A fresh Monday restart each time they slip on the weekend

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Consistency beats heroics. An 80–90% week they can repeat outperforms a perfect week that collapses. Strict-then-free cycles, isolated perfect days, and weekly Monday resets are all-or-nothing patterns, not sustainable coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a reward weekend with sustainability; strict-then-free cycles mimic restrict-binge eating.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses two hero days with a weekly pattern; isolated perfect days are not a repeatable practice.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a Monday reset with consistency; weekly restarts encode all-or-nothing thinking.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: You ask, “On a scale of 1–10, how confident are you that you can do this habit?” You are mainly checking:

options.a: Whether they can recite the biochemistry behind the habit
options.b: Whether guilt is high enough to force compliance this week
options.c: Whether they should add training volume if the habit feels easy
options.d: Whether the habit is sized so they expect to follow through

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: A confidence rating is a sizing tool. Low numbers mean shrink or simplify the habit until they can say 8–9/10. It is not a quiz, a guilt check, or a cue to add CPT training volume. Follow-through tracks expected confidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses confidence with knowledge testing; knowing the science does not mean the habit is doable this week.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses confidence with shame-based compliance; guilt is a poor predictor of repeatable action.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a nutrition-habit check with CPT programming; ease of a food habit is not a reason to add volume.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: You realize you talked for most of a 20-minute check-in. That usually means:

options.a: You were lecturing instead of doing client-centered coaching
options.b: The client still needed more information before they could act
options.c: You built rapport faster by filling silence with your advice
options.d: The session ran efficiently because you covered more content

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: When the coach outtalks the client, the session has slipped into lecturing. Client-centered PN work is mostly asking and listening so they voice the next action. More information, filled silence, and ‘efficient’ content dumps keep ownership with the coach.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a knowledge gap with a reason to monopolize airtime; overload is often why they stop owning the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses talking with rapport; connection grows from listening, not from filling every pause with advice.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses covering topics with coaching; a content-heavy session can still leave the client passive.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: The client’s partner keeps ordering takeout on nights they planned to cook. You treat this as:

options.a: Evidence the client lacks motivation to change their diet
options.b: An environment problem to problem-solve with the client
options.c: A relationship issue outside nutrition coaching altogether
options.d: A willpower test the client must pass without changing dinners

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Household food cues are an environment problem inside coaching scope: change the setup, scripts, or backups around dinner. Blaming motivation, declaring it off-limits as ‘couples therapy,’ or treating it as a willpower exam all miss the 5S supported fix.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an environmental barrier with a motivation deficit; blaming the client ignores the dinner setup.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses household food logistics with therapy you must avoid; dinner environment is squarely in coaching.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses grit with design; willpower against a nightly takeout cue usually fails, so you change the cue.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.prompt: A client wants to overhaul protein, sleep, steps, and alcohol this week. Using PN’s 5S approach, you:

options.a: Launch all four changes together so they feel a complete reset
options.b: Write a periodized lifting mesocycle because this is CPT programming
options.c: Install one simple, supported habit, then sequence the next piece
options.d: Order lab work and a therapeutic diet as if you were their RDN

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: 5S coaching is simple, segmental, sequential, strategic, and supported: one doable habit with support, then the next piece. A four-habit reset, a CPT lifting mesocycle, and RDN-style labs or medical diets all leave that coaching lane.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a full-life reset with 5S sequential change; four new habits at once is not simple or segmental.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses PN Level 1 coaching with CPT programming; periodized lifting is outside this credential’s job.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses coaching with medical nutrition therapy; labs and therapeutic diets belong with an RDN, not L1.
